tierWindow.goal: Work with how university learning, assessment and feedback are designed, so you can act on them in your own study rather than only recognise them.
tierWindow.cognitiveDemand: Application and analysis: interpret, work out and act on settled structures (understand then apply).
tierWindow.taskComplexity: Multi-step but well scaffolded; applying a known framework (constructive alignment, marking criteria, the feedback cycle) to a given case.
tierWindow.autonomy: Moderate scaffolding; a worked example leads, then the learner applies the move; feedback explains and prompts the next step.

decidedValue.priorExperienceAnchor: The learner has met learning, assessment and feedback as a student and can recognise what each is (the introductory tier). They have not yet worked with how these are designed, nor used marking criteria and the feedback cycle deliberately on their own work. This tier puts those skills into action.

decidedValue.courseOutcomeCountReason: Three, matching the three intermediate sub-strands of working with the system: how learning is designed (so you engage with it deliberately), how your work is marked (so you know what it must show), and how feedback is used (so you turn it into improvement). decidedValue.signpostBody: The course has three short lessons. First, how your learning is designed: why sessions are built the way they are, and what that asks of you. Second, reading marking criteria: how to see what a marker is looking for. Third, making feedback work: the cycle that turns comments into better work. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.
decidedValue.signpostInstruction: Work through the three lessons in order.
decidedValue.overview:
This course is about working with how university learning, assessment and feedback are set up, so you can act on them in your own study. By the end you will be able to work out how a module is designed, interpret marking criteria, and use the feedback cycle to turn comments into improvements.

You already know what learning, assessment and feedback are. This course takes the next step: it shows you how they are built, and how to use that knowledge to get more from your course and better marks for your work.
decidedValue.courseOutcomesFraming: Three course outcomes framed up front: work out how learning is designed, interpret marking criteria, use the feedback cycle.

practiceConnection.academic: Working with the system is what separates a student who drifts through modules from one who gets the most out of them. Knowing why a seminar is built as it is, what a marking grid rewards, and how to act on feedback are habits you use in every module, in every subject. Build them now and each assignment becomes easier to target.

grounding.note: W-OPEN states the three course outcomes and why they matter (AL-5)

decidedValue.whereNextBody: Two directions build on this. Going deeper: the advanced course in this pathway takes you into assessing your own and others' work and aligning your whole practice to the learning, assessment and feedback cycle. Going wider: the same habits support Academic Writing, Reflective Practice and Revising and Exams, where you put them to work on real tasks.
decidedValue.summary: You have reached the end of the course. The way your course is built is no longer a mystery you have to guess at. You can work out how a module's learning is designed, and engage with a session in the way it intends. You can read a marking grid and see what each band rewards, so you know what your work needs to show. And you can run the feedback cycle, turning comments into actions that improve the next piece. Look back at the confidence check to see how far this has moved.

practiceConnection.academic: From here, working with the system is something you do in every module. Each time you read a brief against its criteria, prepare for a seminar in the way it is designed, or turn feedback into an action, you are using these habits. They pay off across your degree, and the same ability to read what is wanted and act on it is what professional work rewards too.

courseReferences.title: See Chapters 3, 5 and 6 (pages 36 to 93) of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

items.stem: A workshop is built around a hands-on task you complete in pairs, rather than a talk you listen to. What kind of learning design is this?
Why do tutors decide a session's intended learning outcomes before choosing its activities and content?
In a marking grid, what does a descriptor such as 'developed' or 'basic' tell you?
Work is 'developed' on knowledge but only 'basic' on critical evaluation. How is the overall mark reached?
What is the correct order of the feedback cycle?
A comment says 'you describe sources rather than weighing them'. Which is turning it into an action (Articulate)?
